records.query: key components aircraft fuel servicing safety protocols equipment standards
records.reference: Aircraft fuel servicing involves key components, safety protocols, and equipment standards to ensure safe and efficient fuel transfer. - Fuel Servicing Safety Zone (FSSZ): area within 50 ft of pressurized fuel-carrying servicing components and 25 ft around aircraft fuel vent outlets; active ignition sources (open flames, engine sparks, electrical arcing) must be removed and kept out. Non-servicing vehicles with engines off may park in the FSSZ if they don't block egress.
- Ignition sources: hot surfaces above 750 F and any glowing metal (at least 900 F) are ignition sources; JP-4 vapors ignite from very small sparks; JP-5/JP-8 can ignite when discharged as a mist or spray. Treat any JP-4 spill as flammable.
- Personnel: refueling operations under supervision of the refueling supervisor; no shoes with exposed nails or metal toe/heel plates (nonferrous acceptable); no spark-producing devices in the FSSZ; outer garments with more than 65% nylon, rayon, wool, or polyester not worn in the FSSZ for low-flashpoint fuels (100 F or below); do not don/remove outer garments in the FSSZ.
- Aircraft: non-essential electrical systems, including radar, not activated during servicing unless required; only switches required for concurrent servicing operated.
- Equipment: fire protection per TO 00-25-172 (Table 3-1); deadman controls on approved refueling equipment for ICT operations; vehicles kept at least 25 ft from aircraft fuel vents and pressurized fuel components; external power units parked at least 50 ft from pressurized fuel components and 25 ft from fuel vents, preferably upwind; fuel servicing equipment must conform to TO 37A-1-101 and TO 00-25-172; electric motors within 10 ft of vents/open ports/spills must meet NEC Class I, Division 1 (Zone 1), and elsewhere in the FSSZ Class I, Division 2 (Zone 2).
- Warnings: a malfunction of any fueling system component requires immediate shutdown until repaired. Maintenance/repair of electrical, radio, radar, fuel, or other systems requiring electrical power, and opening lines with flammable or combustible liquids, shall not be accomplished during fueling. Simultaneous fuel and oxygen servicing is not authorized. Electrical power-on portions of -6 or JTD inspections are not authorized during concurrent munitions, reconfiguration, or fuel servicing.

records.query: factors affecting aircraft servicing safety zones
records.reference: Factors affecting aircraft servicing safety zones include the type of aircraft, the type of equipment being used (such as loaders and open-flame heaters), and the specific operation being performed, like concurrent on-offloading/refueling.
records.answer:
The pages describe these factors affecting servicing safety zones: (1) The Fuel Servicing Safety Zone (FSSZ) is the area within 50 feet of a pressurized fuel-carrying servicing component (servicing hose, fuel nozzle, SPR, hydrant hose cart, ramp hydrant connection point, etc.) and 25 feet around aircraft fuel vent outlets; it applies to open ramps and approved hangars/shelters, and is established and maintained during pressurization and fuel movement. (2) Active ignition sources (open flames, internal combustion engine sparks, electrical arcing) must be removed from the FSSZ; non-servicing vehicles and AGE with engines off may be parked there if they do not block egress. (3) Non-essential aircraft electrical systems, including radar, must not be activated during servicing unless required; UHF/VHF cockpit radios may be operated. (4) Adjacent aircraft intruding into the FSSZ must not be involved in engine starts/trim, radiating electromagnetic energy, NDI or welding, energizing/de-energizing external electrical circuits, disconnecting combustible fluid lines (except non-spill quick disconnects), or being moved under power. (5) Aircraft radar and HF radios must not transmit within 300 feet of servicing operations unless specified otherwise; SATCOM may transmit if the antenna beam is at least ten degrees above the horizon. (6) Servicing must not start, or must stop, during a lightning advisory with an electrical storm within five nautical miles, hazardous winds, or fire generating hot ashes in the vicinity; in on-scene fire protection cases, servicing stops during an aircraft crash/fire or in-flight emergency until cleared by the fire authority. (7) Servicing must not start if hot brakes are indicated; fuel servicing does not start until brake temperature is below 750 °F, except for listed exempt aircraft (A-10, C-5, C-17, C-130, E-4, F-15, HH-60; F-22 conditions apply). (8) No smoking within 50 feet of any aircraft or servicing operation. (9) Only personnel required for the operation may remain in the FSSZ, with specified exceptions (aircrew on certain aircraft, trainees under supervision, quality inspectors). (10) Only night vision goggles and intrinsically safe devices may operate within 10 feet of fuel vent outlets, open port receptacles, fuel spills, or fuel trucks being filled; other devices must be turned off within that 10-foot zone. (11) Electric motors for ground heaters/air conditioners must meet NEC Class I Division 1 within 10 feet of vent outlets/spills and Class I Division 2 elsewhere in the FSSZ. (12) Oxygen servicing: the oxygen servicing safety zone requires non-essential persons to stay outside a 20-foot radius, and oxygen servicing must not be done within 50 feet of taxiing aircraft; aircraft electrical systems must not be energized within 25 feet of oxygen servicing. records.query: Explain the components and design of the AFTF.
records.reference: The AFTF (Aircraft Fire Training Facility) is a fixed site simulator for realistic aircraft fire suppression training. It includes a 100-foot burn area, an aircraft mock-up with water-cooled jackets and ignitors, a water pond, and a 10,000-gallon tank for water recycling. The fuel system uses liquid propane (LPG) to simulate multiple fire types, including airframe, engine, and ground fires. The facility is managed via a safety/control stand with electrical, pneumatic, and water systems, and is equipped with manual/pneumatic shutoff valves, an E-stop switch, and fuel shutoff valves for JP-8 and propane for emergency control.
records.answer: The Aircraft Fire Training Facility (AFTF) is a generic site-adaptable design. It consists of an aircraft mock-up, burn area, control stand, compressor shelter, and integrated systems: liquid propane fuel, cathodic (anti-corrosion) protection, pneumatic system, electrical system, and water conservation system with a holding pond incorporating submerged and aeration pumps with associated sprinkler, water jackets, drain and wash down systems. The burn area is a 100-foot (30-meter) lined burn area (underground liner to prevent ground pollution) with a 10,000 water gallon (38,000 liters) liquid propane fuel tank. The aircraft mock-up is constructed of uncoated/unpainted carbon steel, approximately 72 feet long, 25 feet high at tip of tail, with a wingspan of 72 feet, with four simulated aircraft engines (two on the right high wing, one on the vertical stabilizer, and one forward of the left wing known as the Engine Debris trainer), each with a burner assembly and two ignitors. Ignitors are 10,000 volt, 23 milliampere, located in 15 burners. Wiring to mock-up ignitors is enclosed in water jackets. Water injection is in wing engines (and some sites' tail engine); wing engines have dams and plumbing for running fuel fires. Wheel well and APU fires are simulated on the high wing side; interior ignitors/burners simulate cockpit, passenger compartment, and cargo fires. A water sprinkler system along the top of the fuselage cools and washes down the mock-up. Water circulates from the burn area to the environmental pond and back via drains and pumps. An expansion joint is midway on the fuselage. Replaceable 0.031 inch sheet metal cutout panels are on left and right sides, and steel hinged doors are on the left (two) and right (one) sides. Control is via a control stand/control tower, with the facility being a no smoking area.

records.query: Summarize the procedures and safety requirements for removing, packaging, and handling wet and dry batteries from vehicles; mention hazard precautions as well.
records.reference: Wet batteries (except nickel, iron-alkaline) must be removed from vehicles and reported as excess, kept charged, and maintained in a charged condition while awaiting disposal instructions. Dry batteries should be space packaged and packed in accordance with Specification PPP-B-140, with vent holes sealed. Battery posts must be protected using plastic caps or tape conforming to Specification SAE AMS-T-22085. Wet batteries may remain installed in vehicles during military aircraft transport if protected against short circuits by disconnecting and securing cables away from terminals, and properly secured to prevent acid leakage. Dry batteries pose no special hazard and may be installed in the vehicle or shipped with OVE without additional precautions. Wet batteries received with vehicles may be used until the first exercise is completed, after which they must be transferred to a battery room, kept charged, and either shipped or replaced with dry batteries. Dry batteries, whether received charged or not, can be stored in the vehicle’s battery carrier, though indoor storage is preferred, and their vent holes must be sealed until activation. Cable terminals should be greased and taped according to military specifications, and dry batteries must not be activated unless no serviceable wet battery is available. Hazard precautions include preventing acid leakage and short circuits for wet batteries, and ensuring proper handling and activation procedures for dry batteries to avoid chemical exposure.

Packaged batteries and electrolyte are stowed with other OVE, with electrolyte stowed for easy removal at ports when maritime regulations require special stowing. Battery posts are covered with plastic caps or tape conforming to SAE AMS-T-22085. For shipment by military aircraft, wet batteries may remain installed only if completely protected against short circuits (cables removed and ends secured away from terminals) and secured so acid leakage will not occur, and wet batteries shipped with OVE are packed per AFMAN 24-204(IP). Dry batteries offer no special hazard and may be installed in the battery carrier or placed with OVE. records.query: What are the procedures for installing, removing, and requisitioning vehicle markings, including reflective tape?
records.reference: Vehicle markings, including reflective tape, are installed by cleaning the surface, removing the liner, positioning the tape, and applying firm pressure. For removal, pressure-sensitive tape can be softened with heat and isopropyl alcohol (TT-I-735), while older tape requires paint remover (TT-R-2918) or 3M decal remover disks. Markings can be requisitioned through DLA Document Services Online. If decals are unavailable and safety is impacted, stenciling is permitted. Reflectors follow drawing B161059, mounted 24–60 inches above the ground, visible at 100 feet. Install tape according to the steps; damaged areas may be patched.
records.answer: Installing reflectorized tape (P5240, para 2.88): (a) clean the vehicle surface before applying marking; (b) remove liner film down; (c) position emblem on clean surface and tack in position with thumb pressure; (d) start in center using hard overlapping strokes of low friction plastic squeeze; (e) re-squeeze the edges using very firm strokes; (f) apply clean sealer to the edges of the tape; (g) repairs to damaged areas can be made without stripping original tape by cleaning the damaged area and applying new tape over the affected area. Removing reflectorized tape (P5240 para 2.89 WARNING; P5241 paras 2.89.1-2.89.3): WARNING: Lacquer thinner, kylol, and isopropyl alcohol are flammable and toxic. Good general ventilation is normally adequate. Skin and eye protection is required. Avoid all sources of ignition. Failure to comply could result in injury to, or death of, personnel or long term health hazards. Routine removal: soften pressure sensitive tape with heat (heat lamp, heat gun, steam, etc.); soften adhesive residue with rags soaked in isopropyl alcohol, TT-I-735, and scrape away with plastic scraper or putty knife. Old tape: mask off the area, brush paint remover, TT-R-2918, over the tape, applying several times at short intervals and removing residue with plastic scraper or bevel edge putty knife between applications; paint remover may damage paint beneath tape, requiring cleaning and touchup painting. Alternative: use a 4 or 6 inch stripe, molding and decal remover disk (3M), NSN 5130-01-390-9503 (4 inch) or NSN 5130-01-390-9504 (6 inch), with adapter for drill NSN 5130-01-391-2095. NOTE: the solvents are flammable and toxic; take all safety precautions. Requisitioning (P5241 para 2.90): all markings in this chapter can be requisitioned through Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) Document Services via the Document Services Online (DSO) website; once an account is created, process orders through the Travis Plant; DLA Document Services phone (707) 424-0770/(707) 424-4537, DSN 837. NOTE: if decals are not immediately available and the unmarked equipment hampers mission capability or presents a safety hazard, appropriate markings may be stenciled on vehicles prior to receipt of decals. Page P5220 para 2.34 adds that markings must be maintained at all times, with organization markings removed upon transfer within USAF.

records.query: What caution is taken into consideration while using high-pressure wash equipment, and explain the function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit?
records.reference: When using high-pressure wash equipment, caution must be taken to ensure it is never used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attachment points, causing corrosion and wear problems. The function of the portable, 45-gallon, foam-generating cleaning unit is to dispense foam. This cleaning unit is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated, foam-dispensing system that uses the available air supply as its power source to force cleaning solution into the hose and create foam.
records.answer: Caution: High pressure wash equipment developing more than 175 PSI nozzle pressure shall not be used to apply cleaning compounds unless specifically authorized by the equipment System Program Manager (SPM); failure could damage equipment or reduce mission effectiveness. Also, high pressure wash equipment shall never be used on aircraft landing gear and components, wheels, and brakes, as it can force lubricants out of bearings and attach points and cause corrosion and wear. Only low pressure soap nozzles should be used to apply cleaning compounds. Function of the portable 45-gallon foam generating cleaning unit: it is a simplified, portable, pressure-operated foam-dispensing system that uses available air supply as its power source without pumps. Air is metered directly into the pressurized solution chamber, which forces cleaning solution into the hose to create foam. The foam is applied to the surface, allowed to dwell for a minimum of one minute without drying, then scrubbed with a cleaning kit, brush, or cloth and rinsed. Its tank holds 45 gallons, operates at 40-110 PSI compressed air pressure, and requires 15 CFM.

records.query: Define CSO and list down the activities performed in the presence of CSS.
records.reference: Concurrent Servicing Operations (CSO) are the simultaneous servicing of fuel and other aircraft operations such as munitions loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, and aircraft -6 TO inspections. The Chief Servicing Supervisor (CSS) is responsible for on-site supervision of all aspects of concurrent fuel servicing operations. The CSS's activities include ensuring all non-essential personnel and equipment are cleared from the area, briefing team members on duties and emergency procedures, checking the status of the aircraft and its systems with the SCR, ensuring cabin crew have briefed passengers, directing and monitoring the positioning of support equipment and personnel, and having SPR/Vent monitors reposition aircraft wheel chocks as required.
records.answer: CSO (Concurrent Servicing Operations) supporting Combat Sortie Generation (CSG) is the simultaneous fueling, and munitions/ammunition loading/unloading, aircraft reconfiguration, aircraft -6 TO inspections, and other aircraft servicing such as oil, nitrogen, and hydraulic fluid. Oxygen servicing will not be accomplished during fuel servicing. Concurrent servicing (without munitions loading/unloading or aircraft reconfiguration) is the simultaneous servicing of fuel or oxygen with passengers on board or performance of minor maintenance, fleet servicing, or baggage or cargo loading/unloading. Activities requiring a CSS are: refueling/defueling (the key function requiring the CSS); when no refuel/defuel operations take place concurrent with other maintenance/munition tasks, a CSS is not required, and an ATS (not a CSS) is used for ICTs. Per the CSS responsibilities listed: the CSS is responsible for controlling and monitoring all concurrent servicing operations; the CSS checks with the SCR on aircraft and system status and verifies fuel jettison valves are closed before fuel servicing starts; makes sure cabin crew briefed passengers on fuel servicing; directs and monitors support equipment positioning at the aircraft, positioning of the air conditioner outside the FSSZ, positioning of lavatory and portable water trucks, and positioning and bonding of hydrant hose carts or refueling vehicles; remains in constant voice contact with cockpit personnel (when passengers/crew are aboard), SPR/fuel vent monitors and fuel control panel operator; notifies the Fire Department of the number of people on board; and establishes and maintains voice intercom contact if passengers are aboard.
